source.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
source.authors: Danny Hernandez; Tom B. Brown; Tom Conerly; Nova DasSarma; Dawn Drain; Sheer El Showk; Nelson Elhage; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; T. Henighan; Tristan Hume; Scott Johnston; B. Mann; Chris Olah; Catherine Olsson; D. Amodei; Nicholas Joseph; J. Kaplan; Sam McCandlish

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out loss across model sizes and repeated-data conditions, and reports that repetition can produce double descent and departures from power-law scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports copying, prefix-matching, Python evaluation, and fine-tuning results. Only findings that bear on scaling of held-out loss or the repeated-data departures from it are included as rows; copying and mechanistic results are not power-law scaling tests.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own LM scans (about 1.5M–800M parameters, 100B tokens) on unique data and on data with a repeated subset. It reports a good power-law fit for the unique-data control. It shows that repetition bends loss away from that power law (as a function of N) and makes loss rise during training. This bears directly on V1, V5 (repeated data) and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that small repeated fractions at particular frequencies cause severe degradation that scales predictably and occurs in both text and Python. They link it to disproportionate damage to copying and induction heads, and bridge scaling laws with interpretability. They caveat that token count was fixed rather than compute-optimal, region fits are noisy, regularization was not explored, and only loss was measured.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses held-out language-model loss and parameter sweeps, but focuses on repeated-data training, holds training to 100B tokens, and does not test a compute-optimal frontier.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect varies with repetition frequency, repeated-data fraction, model size, and dataset (text versus Python). The authors also state that poor-region boundaries may vary with setup, especially regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: The boundaries of the poor-performance region follow E = k·N^α (right boundary k=5.1e7, α=-0.50; left boundary k=4.2e6, α=-0.56). Extrapolated, they predict degradation from 2x repetition at hundreds of billions of parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The repetition frequency that maximally degrades loss scales as a power law in model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Pretraining on repeated data (73x effective-size loss) leaves a 1.6x effective-size deficit after fine-tuning on Python, worse than training from scratch.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repeated-data pretraining causes ossification that harms later fine-tuning.

record.problems: The study uses a fixed 100B-token budget rather than a compute-optimal frontier. The poor-performance-region fits are described as noisy and are made cleaner by aggregation; the Python fit is noisier still. The text notes that the boundaries may vary with setup, especially regularization. No error bars or confidence intervals are reported in the included results.
record.rows_left_out: Copying and prefix-matching measurements, detailed mechanistic analyses, out-of-distribution Python evaluation of text-trained models, and fine-tuning results are omitted because they do not directly test the listed power-law loss or compute-optimal claims. No more than 60 rows were needed.

untested.parts: Compute scaling; token scaling across separate unique-data runs; scale beyond about 800M parameters.
Entire version: no fit on small runs is validated against larger runs. The extrapolation of poor-region boundaries to GPT-3 scale is not checked.
Image/video modalities, and whether a power-law form holds for fine-tuning or transfer.
Entire version: the authors measured loss only, not downstream tasks.
Parameter counting, schedule choices, fitting method, and compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Python control scan is well fit by a power law in parameters (code trained about 2.2 epochs).
Headline degradation: an 800M model with 10% repeated tokens (0.1% repeated about 100x) has loss near the 340M/400M model, i.e. about a 2x effective-size loss.
Divergence for 12,200 repeated epochs appears around 400M parameters.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. V2 links were removed from r2–r4 because the study never forecasts larger runs from small-run fits. The r5/r6 evidence comes from within-run learning curves, which are weaker evidence on token scaling than separate runs. For r2–r4 and r6 the state is given relative to V1/V5; for V7 the same rows count as observed.

versions.untested_parts: Compute scaling is not measured. The paper does not independently sweep tokens under unique-data training to test token scaling.

There is no direct forecast-validation experiment in which a fit on small runs predicts measured losses of much larger runs. The study compares repeated-data runs with a healthy scaling fit and reports divergence.
No compute-budget sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is tested.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study tests repeated-data training in natural-language and Python models, but not image/video modalities or whether the same law holds in fine-tuning or transfer.
No general downstream-task predictability relationship with scale or pretraining loss is tested.

The study tests departures associated with repeated data and notes noisy fits, but does not systematically compare parameter-counting, fitting, or training-schedule choices, nor compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: control scan (language models trained on unique text)
rows.size_stated: model sizes varied; exact range for this scan not stated
rows.operation_detail: Fit held-out language-model loss against parameter count on the unique-text control scan.
rows.measure: held-out test cross-entropy loss as a function of parameter count
rows.value: The paper states that a power law provides a good fit to the control scan.
rows.note: The result is described for the scan as a whole; no fit coefficients are stated here.
rows.check: Size range is readable from Fig 13 (about 1.5M–800M parameters), not 'not stated'. The Python control fit in the same figure is not recorded.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix A, Figure 13 caption and opening paragraph.

rows.subject: language-model scan (model sizes varied)
rows.operation_detail: Compare held-out loss across parameter counts for runs with repeated training data.
rows.measure: held-out test cross-entropy loss versus parameter count
rows.value: The study reports moderate impact until the model reaches 100M parameters, followed by a large divergence from power-law scaling.
rows.note: The text describes the curve; individual loss values are not given.
rows.check: V2 removed: no fit on small runs is used to forecast larger runs. The condition should read 10% repeated tokens at about 122 repeated epochs; Fig 2 right says 120. State is partial for V1/V5 (power law holds to 100M, then diverges); for V7 the bend is observed.

source_check.correct: State by version: partial for V1/V5; observed for V7, because the reported departure demonstrates setup dependence.
source_check.locator_found: Section 1.1, second bullet; Section 2, Figure 4 caption and accompanying paragraph.
source_check.problem: A single partial state does not fit the linked V7 claim.

rows.subject: language-model scan (model sizes varied)
rows.operation_detail: Measure held-out loss and express the repeated-data loss as an effective model-size multiplier.
rows.measure: held-out test loss, represented as effective model-size multiplier
rows.baseline: control scan used to map test loss to model-size equivalent
rows.value: Performance dips to the equivalent of a model 0.55x as large.
rows.note: The reported multiplier summarizes the dip over the stated parameter range.
rows.check: V2 removed. The 0.55x multiplier is relative to the control power-law fit, so it is a departure. Partial for V1/V5, observed for V7.

source_check.correct: State by version: partial for V1/V5; observed for V7. The text reports 0.55x effective size at 10M–100M parameters with 10% repeated tokens and 1,220 repeats.
source_check.problem: The departure supports V7 rather than partially exhibiting it.

rows.subject: 800M-parameter language model
rows.operation_detail: Measure test loss during training at different repetition frequencies.

conditions.value: varied during the plotted learning curve

rows.value: For some repetition frequencies, test loss decreases, rises during the middle of training, and then decreases again.
rows.note: The paper describes this as a literal double-descent curve; repetition frequencies are varied.
rows.check: Test loss rises mid-training as tokens increase (90% repeated, 100x–10,000x repeats), the opposite of loss falling with tokens. This is a within-run learning curve, not a sweep of separately trained token budgets. Baseline should be the unique-data learning curve.

source_check.correct: State by version: reversed for V1/V5 during the rising-loss interval; observed for V7. The effect occurs at 90% repeated tokens and approximately 100x–10,000x repetition.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 3 caption; Section 2, opening discussion of learning curves.
source_check.problem: Reversed describes loss improvement, but the reversal is affirmative evidence for V7.

rows.subject: 800M-parameter language model
rows.operation_detail: Measure test loss during training at different repetition frequencies.

conditions.value: varied during the plotted learning curve

rows.value: The double-descent bumps become long plateaus for highly affected models.
rows.note: The paper characterizes the plateau as related to epoch-wise double descent.
rows.check: Loss plateaus over a long stretch of tokens at 50% repeated data. This is a within-run learning curve; no baseline is given.

source_check.correct: State by version: partial for V1/V5; observed for V7. Highly affected 800M models with 50% repeated tokens exhibit long test-loss plateaus.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 3 caption; Section 2, opening discussion of learning curves.
source_check.problem: The plateau demonstrates V7's setup-dependent departure rather than partially exhibiting V7.

rows.subject: Python-trained model scan (model sizes varied)
rows.operation_detail: Measure Python test loss across model sizes and repetition frequencies.
rows.value: The paper reports double descent and a poor-performance region; the fit is noisier than for text, and the two boundary lines are no longer parallel.
rows.note: The paper says Python training included approximately 2 epochs of the main dataset, so some repetition also occurred there.
rows.check: The row mainly measures Python loss against repetition frequency (double descent) and the poor-region boundary fit, not loss against N. The Python control power-law fit (Fig 13 right) is the result most relevant to V5 and is not recorded.

source_check.correct: For the reported measure, V5 is cannot_determine: repetition-frequency double descent and noisy boundary fits do not directly establish the form of loss scaling. Setup-dependent curve shapes provide observed evidence relevant to V7. Figure 13 separately reports a good Python control power-law fit.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 11 caption and accompanying Results paragraphs; Appendix A, Figures 13 and 16.
source_check.problem: The row does not directly test the power-law loss form required for a partial V5 state.

relationships.reason: Test loss increases with more training tokens mid-training, a literal double descent (r5).

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.reason: Section 2 explicitly reports test loss increasing mid-training in this regime, reversing improvement as training tokens increase.

relationships.reason: Curves bend away from a single power law depending on the data-repetition setup (r2–r7). The authors say the region boundaries depend on setup and regularization.
relationships.display_finding: Text and Python curves depart from a single power law according to the repetition setup, with region boundaries depending on setup and regularization.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Repetition changes curve shapes and produces departures from the control law; Python exhibits different shapes and noisier boundary fits. Regularization dependence is a caveat, not an experimentally tested result.
